title: Kathina again
hook: the robe offering at the end of the rains

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bon Odori: circles of people moving together at Obon to welcome the ancestors home and send them off again. Your line: dance for them. Who did you move for? Day one thousand fifty-seven.

Every day, through heat and rain, a monk's robe is worn, slept in, washed, mended, and washed again, until it wears out. A monk owns very few things, so the robe is close to everything he has. At the end of the rains retreat, lay people in Theravada countries bring cloth for new robes, at a ceremony called Kathina. This is the third year you've met it. The first time, it was the story of how the offering began. The second, the weaving that runs through the night. Today, the robe itself: how it is sewn, and where it goes after it is given.
screen: `A ROBE WEARS OUT.` → `CLOTH AT THE END OF THE RAINS.` → `WHERE DOES THE ROBE GO?`

segments.voice: Start with the pattern. In the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, the Buddha is walking through the country of Magadha and looks out over the rice fields, laid out in strips with low banks between them. He turns to Ananda and asks whether he could make robes for the monks like that. Ananda can, and does. So the robe is not one smooth length of cloth. It is sewn from cut pieces, set out like fields with borders running between them. The text gives a reason: cloth cut into pieces suits someone who has left home, and nobody would want to steal it. Now follow the robe to its end. Another story in the Vinaya comes after the Buddha has died. The women of King Udena's palace give Ananda a great gift of robes, and the king, puzzled, asks him what he will do with so many. Ananda says he'll give them to monks whose robes are worn thin. And the old robes? They become coverlets. The old coverlets? Mattress covers. The old mattress covers? Rugs for the floor. The old rugs? Cloths for wiping feet. The old foot cloths? Dusters. And the old dusters? Torn into shreds, beaten into clay, and spread as plaster on the floor. Nothing is wasted. That is what the Kathina cloth walks into. It is not a keepsake for a shelf. It becomes a robe that is worn every day, then passed down the line of uses until the last scrap is part of the floor underfoot. That is the shape of the gift: useful, and meant to be used up.
screen: `THE PATTERN OF THE RICE FIELDS.` · `CUT PIECES, SEWN WITH BORDERS.` · `ANANDA ANSWERS THE KING.` · then, large: `USED DOWN TO THE PLASTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: give something useful. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one useful thing you could give: a warm coat you never wear, a good pan, a tool, an hour of help. Not something precious to admire. Something that will get worn. See it in someone else's hands, being used, getting scuffed, wearing thin. Let that be the whole gift, with no say in how it's used and no thank you needed. If you decide to give it, notice how that feels. The bell holds the time.
Kathina again. The cloth offered at the end of the rains, sewn into a robe laid out like rice fields, and used until nothing is left. Today's word.
Your line: the robe given. Today, give one useful thing, something that will be worn out rather than kept, and let it go where it's needed. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries, lay people offer robe cloth and other useful things to monasteries at Kathina ceremonies after the rains retreat ends, and the monks receive the cloth as a community.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. a king asks what you'll do with so many robes, and then what happens to the old ones. what do you say?

pass them down from use to use until even the shreds are used

fork.reveal: Ananda follows the cloth all the way down: coverlets, mattress covers, rugs, foot cloths, dusters, and finally clay plaster for the floor.

original.note: Pali kaṭhina: the name of the robe-cloth offering at the end of the rains.

trapdoor: what you thought: a festival with a robe in it.
what it means: cloth given for a robe that will be worn every day and passed down until it's gone.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's patched robe, laid out like the fields of Magadha, and Ananda's answer to King Udena, which follows the cloth all the way into the floor plaster.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII.12 (robes cut in the pattern of the Magadha rice fields)
Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga XI.1 (Ananda and King Udena: the uses of old robes)

notes: Mahavagga VIII.12: confirm the Buddha sees the Magadha fields (at Dakkhinagiri), asks Ananda, and the stated reason that cut cloth suits samanas and is not coveted by thieves/enemies. Paraphrased, not quoted.

Cullavagga XI.1 (King Udena and Ananda): confirm the sequence robes -> coverlets -> mattress covers -> floor coverings -> foot wipers -> shredded and mixed with clay for plastering. The number of robes in the gift is left out on purpose.
The hook says lay people 'in Theravada countries' bring cloth; no counts or dates used.
Earlier Kathina days (155, 689) told the origin story and the overnight weaving; this day deliberately takes the robe pattern and its afterlife instead.
Original-word stress 'KA-thi-na' is an approximation; please confirm.

Editor pass: restored the dusters step (foot-wipers -> dusters -> shredded into plaster) missing from the Udena sequence; named the givers as the women of King Udena's palace; reworded the hook so it no longer opens 'A [object]...' like the nearby days; cut the claim about what givers know; removed 'first' from the Ananda match pair.

Audit pass: the Cullavagga XI.1 sequence ends with the shreds beaten up with clay and used to plaster the floor (paribhanda), not the walls; teach, match, myth and fork corrected. Confirm against Rhys Davids/Oldenberg (SBE XX).
